slides.0.title: Introducing Austrian wine
slides.0.subtitle: History, the 1985 scandal and recovery
slides.1.title: A long history
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Celts and Romans
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Archaeology points to wine vessels from Celtic culture as early as the 5th century BC; viticulture thrived under the Romans
slides.1.highlights.1.title: The role of monasteries
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Medieval monasteries such as Klosterneuburg drove viticulture, and Charlemagne's rule (from 788) saw major vineyard rebuilding
slides.1.highlights.2.title: The imperial decree of 1784
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Joseph II's decree of 17 August 1784 gave birth to the distinctive Austrian Heuriger (wine tavern) tradition
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Phylloxera
slides.1.highlights.3.content: Phylloxera arrived in 1872 and wiped out most vineyards of central Europe, which were then replanted on grafted rootstocks
slides.1.content: Keep the storyline: an old wine culture → rebuilding after phylloxera → a high-volume 20th century.
slides.2.title: The 20th century: from volume to crisis
slides.2.highlights.0.title: The high-volume era
slides.2.highlights.0.content: In the 20th century Austrian wine became a high-volume, industrialised business, with much sold in bulk to Germany
slides.2.highlights.1.title: A sweeter style
slides.2.highlights.1.content: The market favoured sweeter, fuller wines, and producers chased high-sugar Prädikat levels
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Quality pressure
slides.2.highlights.2.content: The poorly ripened 1982 vintage left some producers unable to meet supermarket contracts requiring Prädikat quality, the background to the 1985 scandal
slides.2.content: The pressure came from the gap between the sweetness contracts demanded and the ripeness actually achieved.
slides.3.title: The 1985 diethylene glycol scandal
slides.3.highlights.0.title: How it was uncovered
slides.3.highlights.0.content: West German labs found it in routine checks: a 1983 Ruster Auslese was analysed on 27 June 1985, and on 9 July the German health ministry issued a warning
slides.3.highlights.1.title: What was added
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Producers added the industrial chemical diethylene glycol to make wines taste sweeter and fuller, imitating late-harvest wines
slides.3.highlights.2.title: The hit to exports
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Exports fell from about 45 million litres a year to roughly 4.4 million in 1986 and only returned to pre-scandal levels in 2001 (figures compiled by Wikipedia)
slides.3.highlights.3.title: The legal response
slides.3.highlights.3.content: Austria's parliament passed a much stricter wine law on 29 August 1985, rushed through to take effect before that year's harvest
slides.3.content: Where figures differ, go by the stated year; the point is "scandal → strict law → turn to quality".
slides.4.title: Recovery and today
slides.4.highlights.0.title: A turn to dry, high quality
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Afterwards Austria shifted to dry whites and higher market segments, regulation tightened sharply and quality became the shared goal
slides.4.highlights.1.title: The start of the DAC system
slides.4.highlights.1.content: The first DAC was Weinviertel (2002 vintage); there are now 18 DACs (see Level 2)
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Scale today
slides.4.highlights.2.content: About 44,000 ha of vines (2024/2025 data), about 25% organic (2025); exports of 60.6 million litres worth about EUR 219 million (2025)
slides.4.content: The year matters: these figures update annually, so they give a sense of scale and are not quiz answers.
In the 1985 scandal, why did producers add diethylene glycol?
B. To make the wine taste sweeter and fuller
It was used to imitate the sweetness and body of late-harvest wines.
Which region was the first DAC?
Weinviertel became the first DAC from the 2002 vintage.
Which Austrian tradition grew out of Joseph II's 1784 decree?
The decree let growers sell their own wine directly, creating the Heuriger tradition.
